claim: Binge drinking alcohol is defined as consuming at least four drinks for women and five drinks for men in a 2 hr drinking session.
source: Binge alcohol consumption, defined as consuming at least four drinks for women and five drinks for men in a 2 hr drinking session, represents a large proportion of the deaths associated with problematic alcohol use and alcohol use disorder (AUD) (Mokdad et al., 2004; Kanny et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mokdad et al., 2004 and Kanny et al., 2018, which are referenced scholarly works.

claim: Binge drinking represents a large proportion of deaths associated with problematic alcohol use and alcohol use disorder.
source: Binge alcohol consumption, defined as consuming at least four drinks for women and five drinks for men in a 2 hr drinking session, represents a large proportion of the deaths associated with problematic alcohol use and alcohol use disorder (AUD) (Mokdad et al., 2004; Kanny et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mokdad et al., 2004 and Kanny et al., 2018.

claim: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults.
source: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults, is behaviorally conserved in rodents, and is a theoretical entry point to the addiction cycle (Thiele and Navarro, 2014; Patrick et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thiele and Navarro, 2014; Patrick et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010.

claim: Binge drinking is behaviorally conserved in rodents.
source: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults, is behaviorally conserved in rodents, and is a theoretical entry point to the addiction cycle (Thiele and Navarro, 2014; Patrick et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thiele and Navarro, 2014; Patrick et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010.

claim: Binge drinking is a theoretical entry point to the addiction cycle.
source: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults, is behaviorally conserved in rodents, and is a theoretical entry point to the addiction cycle (Thiele and Navarro, 2014; Patrick et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thiele and Navarro, 2014; Patrick et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010.

claim: Partaking in binge drinking is one of the strongest predictors for developing alcohol use disorder.
source: Ultimately, partaking in binge drinking is one of the strongest predictors for developing AUD (Addolorato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Addolorato et al., 2018.

claim: Binge drinking alters glutamate receptor function across many brain regions.
source: Previous work has shown binge drinking alters glutamate receptor function across many brain regions (Hwa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hwa et al., 2017.

claim: Ventral tegmental area and thalamic inputs to the extended amygdala have been directly linked to the behavioral control of binge alcohol drinking.
source: Few neural circuits, such as the ventral tegmental area and thalamic inputs to the extended amygdala, locus coeruleus outputs to lateral hypothalamus and rostromedial tegmental nucleus, and medial prefrontal cortex inputs to the periaqueductal gray have been directly linked to the behavioral control of binge alcohol drinking (Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Burnham et al., 2021; Siciliano et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Burnham et al., 2021; Siciliano et al., 2019.

claim: Locus coeruleus outputs to lateral hypothalamus and rostromedial tegmental nucleus have been directly linked to the behavioral control of binge alcohol drinking.
source: Few neural circuits, such as the ventral tegmental area and thalamic inputs to the extended amygdala, locus coeruleus outputs to lateral hypothalamus and rostromedial tegmental nucleus, and medial prefrontal cortex inputs to the periaqueductal gray have been directly linked to the behavioral control of binge alcohol drinking (Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Burnham et al., 2021; Siciliano et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Burnham et al., 2021; Siciliano et al., 2019.

claim: Medial prefrontal cortex inputs to the periaqueductal gray have been directly linked to the behavioral control of binge alcohol drinking.
source: Few neural circuits, such as the ventral tegmental area and thalamic inputs to the extended amygdala, locus coeruleus outputs to lateral hypothalamus and rostromedial tegmental nucleus, and medial prefrontal cortex inputs to the periaqueductal gray have been directly linked to the behavioral control of binge alcohol drinking (Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Burnham et al., 2021; Siciliano et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Burnham et al., 2021; Siciliano et al., 2019.

claim: Clinical and preclinical studies directly implicate a role for the insular cortex in encoding responses to alcohol cues and consumption.
source: Numerous clinical and preclinical studies directly implicate a role for the insular cortex in encoding responses to alcohol cues and consumption (Centanni et al., 2021; Gogolla, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Centanni et al., 2021 and Gogolla, 2017.

claim: Anterior insular cortex inputs to nucleus accumbens core drive aversion-resistant alcohol consumption in rodents.
source: Specifically in rodents, anterior insular cortex (AIC) inputs to nucleus accumbens core have been shown to drive aversion-resistant alcohol consumption and play a role in alcohol discrimination and self-administration (Jaramillo et al., 2018a; Jaramillo et al., 2018b; Seif et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jaramillo et al., 2018a; Jaramillo et al., 2018b; Seif et al., 2013.

claim: Anterior insular cortex inputs to nucleus accumbens core play a role in alcohol discrimination and self-administration in rodents.
source: Specifically in rodents, anterior insular cortex (AIC) inputs to nucleus accumbens core have been shown to drive aversion-resistant alcohol consumption and play a role in alcohol discrimination and self-administration (Jaramillo et al., 2018a; Jaramillo et al., 2018b; Seif et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jaramillo et al., 2018a; Jaramillo et al., 2018b; Seif et al., 2013.

claim: Principal AIC neurons can govern fluid consumption across thirst states that influence voluntary consumption of rewarding substances, such as alcohol.
source: Others have shown that principal AIC neurons can govern fluid consumption across thirst states that influence voluntary consumption of rewarding substances, such as alcohol (Haaranen et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haaranen et al., 2020 and Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: AIC neurons send inputs to many downstream brain regions.
source: Yet, AIC neurons send inputs to many downstream brain regions, so resolving how alcohol alters the functional connectivity by input specificity is of great importance (Gehrlach et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gehrlach et al., 2020.

claim: There is a direct anatomical projection from the AIC to the dorsolateral striatum.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated a direct anatomical projection from the AIC to the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Muñoz et al., 2018; Muñoz et al., 2020; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Muñoz et al., 2018; Muñoz et al., 2020; Wall et al., 2013.

claim: The DLS is a region of striatum that is implicated in alcohol use disorder and behavioral responding for alcohol.
source: The DLS is a region of striatum that is implicated in AUD and behavioral responding for alcohol (Barker et al., 2015; Campbell and Lawrence, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barker et al., 2015 and Campbell and Lawrence, 2021.

claim: Glutamate signaling within the DLS mediates alcohol seeking behaviors.
source: Glutamate signaling within the DLS also mediates alcohol seeking behaviors and alcohol exposure alters excitatory glutamate transmission and synaptic plasticity within the DLS (Corbit et al., 2014; Muñoz et al., 2018; Abburi et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2020; Rangel-Barajas et al., 2021; DePoy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corbit et al., 2014; Muñoz et al., 2018; Abburi et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2020; Rangel-Barajas et al., 2021; DePoy et al., 2013.

claim: Alcohol exposure alters excitatory glutamate transmission and synaptic plasticity within the DLS.
source: Glutamate signaling within the DLS also mediates alcohol seeking behaviors and alcohol exposure alters excitatory glutamate transmission and synaptic plasticity within the DLS (Corbit et al., 2014; Muñoz et al., 2018; Abburi et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2020; Rangel-Barajas et al., 2021; DePoy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corbit et al., 2014; Muñoz et al., 2018; Abburi et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2020; Rangel-Barajas et al., 2021; DePoy et al., 2013.

claim: Glutamatergic synaptic plasticity at AIC inputs to the DLS is uniquely vulnerable to disruption by alcohol exposure, relative to other glutamate synapses within the DLS.
source: We also previously showed that glutamatergic synaptic plasticity at AIC inputs to the DLS (AIC→DLS) is uniquely vulnerable to disruption by alcohol exposure, relative to other glutamate synapses within the DLS (Muñoz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Muñoz et al., 2018.

claim: Animals underwent 3 weeks of the Drinking in the Dark paradigm where they had 0, 2, or 4 hr of access to alcohol or water each day, which produced 'binge-like' levels of alcohol intake.
source: Animals then underwent 3 weeks of the Drinking in the Dark (DID) paradigm where they had 0, 2, or 4 hr of access to alcohol or water each day, which produced 'binge-like' levels of alcohol intake as measured by a positive correlation between alcohol intake and blood alcohol concentration (BAC) with a subset of animals achieving BACs greater than 0.08 mg% (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Thiele and Navarro, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, as well as a citation to Thiele and Navarro, 2014.

claim: There was a positive correlation between alcohol intake and blood alcohol concentration in the DID paradigm.
source: Animals then underwent 3 weeks of the Drinking in the Dark (DID) paradigm where they had 0, 2, or 4 hr of access to alcohol or water each day, which produced 'binge-like' levels of alcohol intake as measured by a positive correlation between alcohol intake and blood alcohol concentration (BAC) with a subset of animals achieving BACs greater than 0.08 mg% (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Thiele and Navarro, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 which shows the correlation data, and a citation to Thiele and Navarro, 2014.

claim: A subset of animals achieved BACs greater than 0.08 mg% in the DID paradigm.
source: Animals then underwent 3 weeks of the Drinking in the Dark (DID) paradigm where they had 0, 2, or 4 hr of access to alcohol or water each day, which produced 'binge-like' levels of alcohol intake as measured by a positive correlation between alcohol intake and blood alcohol concentration (BAC) with a subset of animals achieving BACs greater than 0.08 mg% (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Thiele and Navarro, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and a citation to Thiele and Navarro, 2014.

claim: Binge alcohol consumption increased optically evoked postsynaptic current amplitude of AIC inputs within the DLS.
source: (E) Binge alcohol consumption increased optically evoked postsynaptic current (oEPSC) amplitude of AIC inputs within the DLS (two-way mixed analysis of variance (ANOVA), Fluid F(1,50) = 15.6084, p=0.0002; Fluid × Light Intensity F(5,250) = 6.0674, p=0.000025; alcohol: 26 recordings, n=5 animals; water: 26 recordings, n=6 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Binge alcohol consumption reduced optically evoked AMPA to NMDA glutamate receptor current ratios.
source: (F) Binge alcohol consumption reduced optically evoked AMPA (oAMPA) to NMDA (oNMDA) glutamate receptor current ratios (Mann-Whitney, U=189, p=0.0072; alcohol: 24 recordings, n=5 animals; water: 28 recordings, n=6 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There was no main effect of binge alcohol consumption on paired-pulse ratios of oEPSCs compared to water consumption.
source: (G) There was no main effect of binge alcohol consumption on paired-pulse ratios of oEPSCs (oPPR) compared to water consumption (two-way mixed ANOVA, Fluid F(1,55) = 2.5544, p=0.1157; alcohol: 30 recordings, n=6 animals; water: 27 recordings, n=5 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Binge drinking alcohol decreased optically evoked population spike amplitudes produced by photoexciting AIC inputs within the DLS.
source: (H) Binge drinking alcohol decreased optically evoked population spike (oPS) amplitudes produced by photoexciting AIC inputs within the DLS (two-way mixed ANOVA, Fluid F(1,28) = 4.3484, p=0.0463; Fluid × Light Intensity F(6,168) = 2.9574, p=0.0090; alcohol: 14 recordings, n=4 animals; water: 16 recordings, n=6 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Alcohol can have synapse-specific effects in dorsal striatum, which are otherwise obscured by the net effects at other synapses when synaptic transmission is measured in a non-circuit-specific manner.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we have shown that alcohol can have synapse-specific effects in dorsal striatum, which are otherwise obscured by the net effects at other synapses when synaptic transmission is measured in a non-circuit-specific manner (Muñoz et al., 2018; Muñoz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Muñoz et al., 2018 and Muñoz et al., 2020.

claim: Binge drinking alcohol selectively potentiates postsynaptic AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptor responses at AIC→DLS synapses.
source: Specifically, these data indicate that binge drinking alcohol selectively potentiates postsynaptic AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptor responses at AIC→DLS synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Binge alcohol consumption decreased sEPSC amplitudes compared to water drinkers.
source: (A) Binge alcohol consumption decreased sEPSC amplitudes compared to water drinkers (Mann-Whitney, U=247.5, p=0.0441; alcohol: 27 recordings, n=6 animals; water: 27 recordings, n=5 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Female mice that binge drank alcohol compared to water drinking controls show no changes in oEPSC amplitude, oAMPA/oNMDA ratio, or oPPR.
source: Interestingly, female mice that binge drank alcohol compared to water drinking controls show no changes in oEPSC amplitude, oAMPA/oNMDA ratio, or oPPR (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D-F.

claim: With both males and female datasets combined, there was a significant fluid effect, but not a significant fluid by sex effect for oEPSC amplitude.
source: With both males and female datasets combined, we found a significant fluid effect, but not a significant fluid by sex effect for oEPSC amplitude (three-way mixed analysis of variance [ANOVA], Fluid F(1,75) = 8.309, p=0.0051; Fluid × Sex F(1,75) = 3.044, p=0.0851).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of combined male and female experimental data.

claim: For oAMPA/oNMDA ratios, there was a sex effect driven by binge alcohol exposed male mice.
source: For oAMPA/oNMDA ratios, we discovered a sex effect driven by binge alcohol exposed male mice (two-way ANOVA, Sex F(1,80) = 5.8532, p=0.0178; Fluid × Sex F(1,80) = 7.2132, p=0.0088).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of combined male and female experimental data.

claim: The observed synaptic plasticity changes measured were present only in male mice.
source: Since the observed synaptic plasticity changes measured were present only in male mice, we chose to focus on males for further AIC focused circuit-specific and behavioral analyses, but other female circuit-specific alterations need to be explored in future studies.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing differences between male and female mice.

claim: oPS amplitudes were decreased in male mice that binge drank alcohol compared to water.
source: oPS amplitudes were decreased in male mice that binge drank alcohol compared to water (Figure 1H), indicating that the net effect of binge alcohol-induced AIC→DLS synaptic adaptations is a reduced network response to AIC input activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The net effect of binge alcohol-induced AIC→DLS synaptic adaptations is a reduced network response to AIC input activation.
source: oPS amplitudes were decreased in male mice that binge drank alcohol compared to water (Figure 1H), indicating that the net effect of binge alcohol-induced AIC→DLS synaptic adaptations is a reduced network response to AIC input activation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: A single alcohol DID exposure increased oEPSC amplitude compared to water controls.
source: A single alcohol DID exposure increased oEPSC amplitude compared to water controls, a finding consistent with 3 weeks of DID exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E.

claim: A single DID session did not produce changes in oAMPA/oNDMA ratio and oPS amplitudes.
source: Yet, there were no changes in oAMPA/oNDMA ratio and oPS amplitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5F and G.

claim: A single DID exposure is not sufficient to recapitulate the AIC→DLS circuit changes seen after 3 weeks of DID exposure.
source: This suggests that a single DID exposure is not sufficient to recapitulate the AIC→DLS circuit changes seen after 3 weeks of DID exposure.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of single session and 3-week DID experimental data.

claim: Enhanced glutamate transmission at AIC inputs to DLS may drive local inhibitory networks leading to overall decreased MSN activity.
source: Together, these data indicate that enhanced glutamate transmission at AIC inputs to DLS may drive local inhibitory networks leading to overall decreased MSN activity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: AIC inputs equally innervate different types of MSNs.
source: AIC inputs equally innervate different types of MSNs indicating that this effect is not due to a preferential engagement of one type of MSN (Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wall et al., 2013.

claim: AIC inputs may induce feedforward inhibition through local interneurons, such as engaging fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Other possibilities are that AIC inputs induce feedforward inhibition through local interneurons, such as engaging fast-spiking interneurons, which have been implicated in compulsive alcohol consumption (Patton et al., 2021; Manz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Patton et al., 2021 and Manz et al., 2020.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons have been implicated in compulsive alcohol consumption.
source: Other possibilities are that AIC inputs induce feedforward inhibition through local interneurons, such as engaging fast-spiking interneurons, which have been implicated in compulsive alcohol consumption (Patton et al., 2021; Manz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Patton et al., 2021 and Manz et al., 2020.

claim: Alterations in DLS neurotransmission are known to facilitate the development of habit learning in the context of substance-related behaviors.
source: Alterations in DLS neurotransmission are known to facilitate the development of habit learning in the context of substance-related behaviors and are also associated with the expression of numerous alcohol-related behaviors (Koob and Volkow, 2010; Lovinger and Alvarez, 2017; Corbit et al., 2012; Patton et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koob and Volkow, 2010; Lovinger and Alvarez, 2017; Corbit et al., 2012; Patton et al., 2016.

claim: Alterations in DLS neurotransmission are associated with the expression of numerous alcohol-related behaviors.
source: Alterations in DLS neurotransmission are known to facilitate the development of habit learning in the context of substance-related behaviors and are also associated with the expression of numerous alcohol-related behaviors (Koob and Volkow, 2010; Lovinger and Alvarez, 2017; Corbit et al., 2012; Patton et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koob and Volkow, 2010; Lovinger and Alvarez, 2017; Corbit et al., 2012; Patton et al., 2016.

claim: Glutamate receptor signaling specifically within the DLS mediates alcohol seeking behavior.
source: Glutamate receptor signaling specifically within the DLS mediates alcohol seeking behavior (Corbit et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corbit et al., 2014.

claim: Licks, bouts, and total lick duration metrics from the lickometers were significantly correlated with water and alcohol intakes.
source: Licks, bouts, and total lick duration metrics from the lickometers were significantly correlated with water and alcohol intakes and thus provided high-resolution drinking microstructure details about how and when during each DID session each animal consumed water or alcohol (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: During binge acquisition (weeks 1–3), there were baseline differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls for water, but not alcohol intake.
source: During binge acquisition (weeks 1–3), there were baseline differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls for water, but not alcohol intake (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: There was no change in water intake between ChR2 and eGFP controls during binge evaluation (weeks 4–6).
source: For binge evaluation (weeks 4–6), there was no change in water intake between ChR2 and eGFP controls (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ChR2 expressing animals drank significantly less alcohol than eGFP controls during binge evaluation.
source: Yet, contrary to our initial hypothesis, ChR2 expressing animals drank significantly less alcohol than eGFP controls. Thus, driving glutamate release from AIC inputs within the DLS selectively decreased binge drinking in animals that consumed alcohol, but not water (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Driving glutamate release from AIC inputs within the DLS selectively decreased binge drinking in animals that consumed alcohol, but not water.
source: Yet, contrary to our initial hypothesis, ChR2 expressing animals drank significantly less alcohol than eGFP controls. Thus, driving glutamate release from AIC inputs within the DLS selectively decreased binge drinking in animals that consumed alcohol, but not water (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The in vivo optical stimulation did not induce differential plasticity in water and alcohol drinkers.
source: This was not a product of the in vivo optical stimulation inducing differential plasticity in water and alcohol drinkers. Testing the same stimulation pattern used in vivo in brain slices did not produce different effects in slices from water and alcohol drinkers or induce long-lasting glutamatergic plasticity on its own, even in the presence of the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Alcohol-induced plasticity changes at AIC inputs to DLS are a prerequisite for decreasing alcohol intake.
source: We reasoned that since driving glutamate release during water DID sessions did not alter intakes, that alcohol-induced plasticity changes at AIC inputs to DLS were a prerequisite for decreasing alcohol intake.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Photoexciting AIC inputs to the DLS during binge acquisition did not alter alcohol intakes compared to non-photoexcited alcohol drinkers.
source: To confirm, we photoexcited AIC inputs to the DLS in a separate cohort of animals during binge acquisition (sessions 1–15) to see if animals would decrease their intakes or not acquire stable alcohol intakes. These animals did not show any differences between non-photoexcited alcohol drinkers suggesting alcohol-induced AIC→DLS plasticity changes are necessary to alter binge alcohol intakes (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Alcohol-induced AIC→DLS plasticity changes are necessary to alter binge alcohol intakes.
source: These animals did not show any differences between non-photoexcited alcohol drinkers suggesting alcohol-induced AIC→DLS plasticity changes are necessary to alter binge alcohol intakes (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: For water drinkers, there were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls in licks, lick duration, bouts, latency to drink, mean inter-drink interval, or bouts in the first 30 min of each DID session.
source: For water drinkers, there were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls in licks, lick duration, bouts, latency to drink, mean inter-drink interval, or bouts in the first 30 min of each DID session (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: For alcohol drinkers, there were significant decreases in licks, lick duration, and bouts in ChR2 compared to eGFP controls.
source: As expected for alcohol drinkers, there were significant decreases in licks, lick duration, and bouts in ChR2 compared to eGFP controls (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: For alcohol latency to drink and mean inter-drink-interval, there were no significant effects between groups.
source: For alcohol latency to drink and mean inter-drink-interval, there were no significant effects between groups (Figure 3J and K), but the number of alcohol bouts in the first 30 min (a measurement of 'front-loading' behavior) decreased for ChR2 compared to eGFP controls (Figure 3L; Wilcox et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: The number of alcohol bouts in the first 30 min decreased for ChR2 compared to eGFP controls.
source: For alcohol latency to drink and mean inter-drink-interval, there were no significant effects between groups (Figure 3J and K), but the number of alcohol bouts in the first 30 min (a measurement of 'front-loading' behavior) decreased for ChR2 compared to eGFP controls (Figure 3L; Wilcox et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L and a citation to Wilcox et al., 2014.

claim: A feedforward artificial neural network achieved an average of 66.13% accuracy on data previously unseen by the model to predict fluid type and viral expression from a single DID session solely from microstructure data.
source: After splitting our dataset into training and testing sets, performing sixfold stratified cross-validation (to ensure each training fold had a representative proportion of fluid type and viral expression samples), and training the network we achieved an average of 66.13% accuracy (2.6 times better than chance accuracy) on data previously unseen by the model to predict fluid type and viral expression from a single DID session solely from microstructure data (Figure 3N–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by machine learning analysis results shown in Figure 3N-O.

claim: The neural network accuracy was 2.6 times better than chance accuracy.
source: After splitting our dataset into training and testing sets, performing sixfold stratified cross-validation (to ensure each training fold had a representative proportion of fluid type and viral expression samples), and training the network we achieved an average of 66.13% accuracy (2.6 times better than chance accuracy) on data previously unseen by the model to predict fluid type and viral expression from a single DID session solely from microstructure data (Figure 3N–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by machine learning analysis results.

claim: AIC inputs within the DLS govern binge alcohol-related behaviors so strongly that experimental manipulations can be reliably predicted based on how animals consume fluid from a DID session.
source: Thus, AIC inputs within the DLS govern binge alcohol-related behaviors so strongly that we can reliably predict which animals received specific experimental manipulations based on how they consume fluid from a DID session.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the machine learning analysis results.

claim: Alcohol-induced neuroplasticity at AIC inputs to DLS may serve as a gain-of-function that allows these synapses to maintain alcohol consumption.
source: Altogether, our drinking data indicate that alcohol-induced neuroplasticity at AIC inputs to DLS may serve as a gain-of-function that allows these synapses to maintain alcohol consumption.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In the absence of alcohol, AIC→DLS synapses seem to play no role in modulating intake behaviors.
source: In the absence of alcohol, these synapses seem to play no role in modulating intake behaviors, likely due to the absence of a specific type of plasticity required to engage or bring these synapses 'online'.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing no effect on water intake.

claim: Once alcohol-induced plasticity at AIC→DLS synapses occurs, it likely enables the governance of alcohol drinking behaviors via complex control over the patterns of licking behavior.
source: Once alcohol-induced plasticity at these synapses occurs, it likely enables the governance of alcohol drinking behaviors via complex control over the patterns of licking behavior.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Binge-like sucrose consumption did not produce the same effect on AIC-DLS synaptic plasticity as alcohol.
source: We note that in our previous work binge-like sucrose consumption did not produce the same effect on AIC-DLS synaptic plasticity as alcohol (Muñoz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Muñoz et al., 2018.

claim: There were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls for time in zone or distance traveled in the real-time place preference assay.
source: There were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls for time in zone or distance traveled, suggesting photoexciting AIC inputs to the DLS does not alter preference/avoidance behaviors or locomotion (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Photoexciting AIC inputs to the DLS does not alter preference/avoidance behaviors or locomotion.
source: There were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls for time in zone or distance traveled, suggesting photoexciting AIC inputs to the DLS does not alter preference/avoidance behaviors or locomotion (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: There were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls in time spent on the light side of the box across LED epochs, total number of light side entries, or latency to enter the dark side in the light-dark test.
source: There were no differences between ChR2 and eGFP controls in time spent on the light side of the box across LED epochs, total number of light side entries, or latency to enter the dark side (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: There were no group differences between nosepoking behaviors for photoexcitation in the intracranial self-stimulation assay.
source: There were no group differences between nosepoking behaviors for photoexcitation (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Modulating AIC inputs within the DLS does not decrease alcohol intake via changes in reward perception, valence, reinforcement, locomotion, or anxiety-like behavior.
